retrieved.title: TRL 2 — Technology concept formulated
retrieved.content: Once basic principles are observed, practical applications can be speculated upon, but they remain analytic; no experimental proof or detailed analysis yet supports the invention. For a startup, this looks like a named product concept and an architecture sketch describing how the underlying principle would solve a specific problem, backed by rough back-of-envelope reasoning rather than any built code or lab result.
retrieved.citation: European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme, General Annex B — Technology Readiness Levels (TRL); consistent with ISO 16290:2013

retrieved.title: TRL 3 — Experimental proof of concept
retrieved.content: Active research and development is initiated, including analytical and laboratory studies to physically validate the analytical predictions of separate elements of the technology. For a startup, this means a scoped experiment or a proof-of-concept script has produced a recorded result showing the core mechanism functions in isolation, even though no components have been integrated into a working prototype.
retrieved.citation: European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme, General Annex B — Technology Readiness Levels (TRL); consistent with ISO 16290:2013

retrieved.title: MRL 3 — Informal problem interviews
retrieved.content: The team has held informal conversations with prospective buyers — problem interviews or casual conversations at events — surfacing anecdotal interest, but no prospect has made any commitment. Evidence is a set of interview notes or call logs showing a handful of conversations, with reactions recorded but no willingness-to-pay signal.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: MRL 4 — Structured customer discovery
retrieved.content: Customer discovery has been formalized: structured interviews have been run across multiple prospects using a consistent script, and a common pain point has been validated across that sample. Evidence is a discovery report summarizing interview themes across a named number of prospects, though no prospect has yet indicated a specific willingness to pay.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: RRL 1 — No regulatory analysis
retrieved.content: No analysis has been done of which laws, regulations, or licensing regimes apply to the product or its operation; the regulatory landscape is entirely unknown to the team. Evidence at this level is the absence of any regulatory review — no memo, no advisor engaged, no list of candidate rules.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: RRL 2 — Regulatory domain identified
retrieved.content: The team has identified which regulatory domain and which oversight body plausibly governs the product — for example, data protection, financial services, or medical device rules — but has not obtained any formal legal assessment of what specifically applies. Evidence is an internal note naming the likely regulator or regulatory area, based on the team's own research rather than counsel.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: ARL 3 — Informal demo reactions
retrieved.content: The product concept has been shown to a handful of prospective users through informal demos, and their verbal reactions have been captured, but no behavior has actually been measured — reactions are qualitative impressions only. Evidence is a log of demo sessions with recorded verbal feedback from a small number of people.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: ARL 4 — Structured usability testing
retrieved.content: Structured usability or concept-testing sessions have been run with prospective users, collecting task-completion and satisfaction data, but every interaction has occurred under direct observation rather than independent use. Evidence is a usability test report with task-completion rates and satisfaction scores from a defined set of observed sessions.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: ORL 2 — Informal division of responsibilities
retrieved.content: Founders have informally divided responsibilities between themselves based on skill or interest, but nothing is written down and decisions are still made ad hoc rather than through any agreed process. Evidence is, at most, an informal verbal understanding of who handles what, with no written role description or org chart.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: ORL 3 — First non-founder contributor
retrieved.content: A first contributor beyond the founders — a contractor, advisor, or part-time hire — has joined the venture, but there is still no formal governance structure or documented operating process guiding how work happens. Evidence is a contract or engagement letter for the first non-founder contributor, with no accompanying process documentation.

retrieved.title: TRL 6 — Technology demonstrated in relevant environment
retrieved.content: A representative model or prototype system, well beyond the level tested for TRL 5, is tested in a relevant environment, going beyond laboratory testing to simulated operational conditions. A startup at this level has run a pilot with a small number of real customers in their own environment, delivering an end-to-end result and capturing structured feedback, though the deployment is limited in scale and duration.
retrieved.citation: European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme, General Annex B — Technology Readiness Levels (TRL); consistent with ISO 16290:2013

retrieved.title: TRL 7 — System prototype demonstration in operational environment
retrieved.content: A prototype implementation, near or at the scale of the planned operational system, is demonstrated in an actual operational environment. For a startup, this looks like a substantially complete version of the product running live for real customers under actual operating conditions, in a limited rollout rather than a full launch, with monitoring in place to capture how it behaves outside a controlled trial.
retrieved.citation: European Commission, Horizon Europe Work Programme, General Annex B — Technology Readiness Levels (TRL); consistent with ISO 16290:2013

retrieved.title: MRL 5 — Paid pilots with named customers
retrieved.content: Demand has moved from stated interest to a financial commitment: the startup has run repeated paid pilots with named customers, each willing to pay for a defined trial period. Evidence is signed pilot agreements or purchase orders from more than one named customer, together with pilot usage or outcome data collected during the engagement.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: MRL 6 — Repeat sales beyond initial pilots
retrieved.content: The customer base has expanded beyond the original pilots — additional paying customers have been acquired using a pitch or process that is starting to repeat — but there is no scalable acquisition channel yet and each sale still depends heavily on founder involvement. Evidence is a growing list of paying customers with dates of acquisition, plus early renewal or expansion revenue from at least one pilot customer.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: RRL 1 — No regulatory analysis
retrieved.content: No analysis has been done of which laws, regulations, or licensing regimes apply to the product or its operation; the regulatory landscape is entirely unknown to the team. Evidence at this level is the absence of any regulatory review — no memo, no advisor engaged, no list of candidate rules.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: RRL 2 — Regulatory domain identified
retrieved.content: The team has identified which regulatory domain and which oversight body plausibly governs the product — for example, data protection, financial services, or medical device rules — but has not obtained any formal legal assessment of what specifically applies. Evidence is an internal note naming the likely regulator or regulatory area, based on the team's own research rather than counsel.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: ARL 5 — Measured usage by trial users
retrieved.content: Real users beyond the founding team have used the product independently in a trial, and their usage has actually been measured rather than merely observed. Evidence is trial usage data — session logs, feature-usage counts, or completion events — captured from named non-founder users without the founders present.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: ARL 6 — Repeat usage and first referrals
retrieved.content: The trial cohort has expanded and users are returning for repeat sessions rather than trying the product once, with engagement metrics such as return rate now tracked, and the first organic, unprompted referrals from users to their peers have begun to appear. Evidence is a return-rate metric across a named trial cohort plus at least one documented organic referral.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: ORL 2 — Informal division of responsibilities
retrieved.content: Founders have informally divided responsibilities between themselves based on skill or interest, but nothing is written down and decisions are still made ad hoc rather than through any agreed process. Evidence is, at most, an informal verbal understanding of who handles what, with no written role description or org chart.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: ORL 3 — First non-founder contributor
retrieved.content: A first contributor beyond the founders — a contractor, advisor, or part-time hire — has joined the venture, but there is still no formal governance structure or documented operating process guiding how work happens. Evidence is a contract or engagement letter for the first non-founder contributor, with no accompanying process documentation.
retrieved.citation: Balanced Readiness Level assessment (BRLa), Technological Forecasting and Social Change (2021) — dimension framework; level descriptors authored against its stated criteria

retrieved.title: IRL 1 — No funding plan, founder time only
retrieved.content: No funding plan exists at all: the venture is running on founder time and personal resources with no target raise amount, no use-of-funds outline, and no investor contact of any kind. Evidence is simply the absence of any funding document or investor conversation.

retrieved.title: IRL 2 — Informal funding hypothesis
retrieved.content: An informal funding hypothesis has been noted — a general sense that a seed round will eventually be needed — but no target amount, use-of-funds outline, or investor list has been drafted. Evidence is, at most, a passing mention in founder notes rather than any funding document.

byDim.Technology: MediSync Cebu transmits structured referral records with bed availability, triage category, and attached history. It progressed from a Feb 2025 pilot with 2 RHUs and 1 district hospital to 6 facilities by Aug 2025. To serve the broader market of 44 RHUs, 8 district hospitals, and 3 tertiary centers in Cebu, the system needs expanded operational deployment and integration across larger facility networks.
byDim.Market: Targeting 44 rural health units, 8 district hospitals, and 3 tertiary referral centres in Cebu, the venture secured its first paid facility subscriptions in Aug 2025 and reached PHP 5,000 monthly recurring revenue by Feb 2026 across 6 facilities. To grow beyond initial paid customers, the venture needs to establish repeat sales processes and acquire additional paying facilities.
byDim.Acceptance: The system replaces paper forms and phone calls, expanding from an initial 3-facility trial cohort to 6 operational facilities. To further validate user acceptance, the team needs to systematically measure independent user session logs, return rates, feature usage, and organic user referrals among clinical staff.
byDim.Organizational: The team grew to 3 founders: Dr. Elena Reyes (9 years provincial public health), Marco Villanueva (7 years health IT), and Joy Tabotabo (5 years LGU administration). Operating with an informal division of responsibilities, the team needs to document roles, formalize decision processes, and bring on its first non-founder contributors.
byDim.Regulatory: No patents exist, and a trademark application is pending with IPOPHL. No formal regulatory analysis has been performed regarding applicable public health, medical data, or data privacy rules. The venture needs to identify relevant regulatory bodies and conduct a legal assessment of compliance requirements.
byDim.Investment: The venture generates PHP 5,000 monthly recurring revenue but lacks a funding plan, relying on founder time and resources. The team needs to articulate a funding hypothesis, determine target raise requirements and use of funds, and initiate contact with prospective investors.
